title: Which freeze-dried foods survive a backpack.
description: What breaks in a pack, what only looks broken — published fragility statements, the fat problem, and the puncture figures no maker publishes.

faq.question: Which freeze-dried foods are the most fragile in a pack?
faq.answer: No source publishes a ranking, and that is worth saying plainly rather than filling in. The only food any primary source names for crush risk is leafy greens: "Leafy greens are light after drying, so handle and package them carefully to prevent crushing" [1]. Everything else in the fragility column of the table above is either an inference from a published preparation instruction or an absence. A ranked list of fragile foods circulating anywhere is somebody's estimate, not published data.

faq.question: Does it matter if my fruit arrives at camp as powder?
faq.answer: For eating dry it matters; for rehydration the published guidance does not distinguish. Fruit is rehydrated by soaking in a bowl, spritzing, or adding water a little at a time [6], and none of those methods specify an intact piece. Freeze-dried meat is described as reabsorbing "only the liquid it needs" regardless of form [7]. The practical loss from crushing is texture and portioning, not rehydration — but no source has tested crushed versus intact pieces side by side.

faq.question: Can I take freeze-dried cheese, bacon, or nut butter backpacking?
faq.answer: They freeze dry, with a documented storage penalty. Harvest Right names cheese, bacon, sausage, butter, peanut butter, salmon and avocados as high-fat cautions that "can still be freeze dried successfully, but they typically won't store as long" [3], and separately states that higher-fat foods have shorter storage lives because fats oxidize [4]. Extension is firmer: high fat "increases the risk of rancidity during storage," and high-fat cheese should be melted or blended and spread thinly before drying [8]. UC Cooperative Extension advises avoiding oily foods including butter, peanut butter and chocolate outright [10]. Nobody publishes a fat percentage that separates the two positions.

faq.question: How long can a repackaged pouch ride in a pack before the fat is a problem?
faq.answer: No source answers this for freeze-dried food. The nearest published figure is for a different process entirely: NCHFP states that properly dried jerky "will keep at room temperature two weeks in a sealed container" and instructs trimming all fat because "it becomes rancid quickly" [11]. That is a dehydrated-meat figure and it is not transferable to a freeze-dried pouch. A commercial brand offers the only other datapoint on the direction of the effect: its three-year SKUs "typically have higher fat or dairy content" against ten years for the rest of its line [12]. Direction is well sourced; duration on the trail is not.

faq.question: Should I repackage store-bought pouches into lighter bags?
faq.answer: No source addresses repackaging, in either direction. What is published is the barrier and durability side: mylar sold for freeze-dried food runs 2.0–7.5 mil, with "Heavy Duty" grades starting at 7.0 mil [16], and one seller states that bags under 5 mil do not provide adequate protection from UV [17]. Mountain House warns against storage conditions that could puncture or dent its packaging [13]. Whether transferring food out of a factory pouch into a thinner bag changes crush or puncture outcomes is untested by anyone, and neither the pouch brands nor the bag manufacturers publish a number you could use to decide.

bodyHtml:
The short version: freeze-dried food is fragile because almost nothing shrinks around the space the water left — Clemson puts the shrinkage of freeze-dried food at 5–15%, against around 80% for air drying [21], so what you carry is a full-size piece of food that is mostly void. Nothing in the published literature ranks foods by how well they survive a pack, and only one food is named anywhere for crush risk. Fat is the better-documented trail problem: it does not sublimate, and every tier of source agrees it shortens storage life, though none of them publishes a threshold.

Why some foods break

Freeze drying removes water without collapsing the structure that held it. Clemson's figure is the clearest published statement of that difference: 5–15% shrinkage for freeze-dried food, around 80% for air drying [21]. Air-dried fruit is dense and leathery because the cell walls pulled inward; freeze-dried fruit keeps its original dimensions with the water replaced by air. That is the same property that makes it rehydrate quickly and the same property that makes it break in a loaded pack.

Manufacturers treat the brittleness as the doneness signal, not a defect. Correctly finished product is described as "crisp or brittle" and "easy to break, crumble, or crush when appropriate" [1]. Anything that reads as still soft or leathery in the center is under-dried, so a batch that survives a pack because it is bendy is a batch that was not finished.

Two structural cases are documented separately. Skins resist drying — "any food with a skin will have a harder time freeze drying," with blueberries called out as especially difficult, and the published order of preference is purée, then halve or quarter, then pierce with a toothpick [19]. University of Arizona Extension gives the same instruction for a different reason: "cranberries or blueberries need to be punctured to prevent them from bursting" [20]. Neither side addresses the other's mechanism, and either way you arrive at camp with a pierced or halved berry rather than a whole one.

The other case is leafy greens, and it is the only food any primary source names for crush risk in storage: "Leafy greens are light after drying, so handle and package them carefully to prevent crushing" [1]. No source names a second food, and no source at any tier ranks foods by crush, shatter or compression risk. A fragility ordering would have to be invented, so there is not one below.

What the sources actually say, food by food

Every cell is what a manufacturer or extension service publishes. Blank cells are absences, not omissions — they are listed again at the end.

FoodFragility, as publishedWhat breaks, and whyStill rehydrates?
Leafy greens The only food named for crush risk by any primary source: "light after drying, so handle and package them carefully to prevent crushing" [1] Thin cell structure with nothing to compress around; the piece is almost entirely void after drying [21] Yes, and by a method that does not need an intact leaf — spritz with water, or seal in a bag with a moist paper towel [6]
Berries with skins (blueberries, cranberries, grapes) Not published. The published handling concern is drying, not carrying The prep itself opens them: purée, halve or quarter, or pierce [19], because whole skins block moisture escape [19] or burst [20]. You start from a broken piece Yes — soak in a bowl, spritz, or add water gradually [6]. Many are eaten dry without rehydrating [6]
Sliced fruit (apples, strawberries, bananas) Not published. No fragility figure, no comparison against other foods The structural property is general, not fruit-specific: 5–15% shrinkage leaves a full-volume, mostly-air piece [21] Yes — soak, spritz, or add water a little at a time [6]; fruit for baking can go in dry and rehydrate during cooking [6]
Cooked meat pieces Not published. The published constraints are thickness and fat, not durability Prep sets the piece size: trim visible fat and bone, cut no thicker than about ¾ inch [20] Yes — and form appears not to matter: freeze-dried meat "will only reabsorb the liquid it needs, it will never become soggy" [7]. Meat mixes take about ⅓ hot water by volume [7]. Raw meat must be rehydrated in cold water in the refrigerator and then cooked [8]
Cooked meals and casseroles Not published. Fragility is unaddressed for mixed dishes Guidance is about drying evenly, not surviving transport: portion before drying rather than drying a whole casserole, keep pieces ¼–½ inch [3]. Arizona adds that mixed foods dry well "if they are not overly greasy" [20] Yes. Add hot water gradually, stir, cover and rest [6][7]
High-fat items (cheese, bacon, sausage, nut butter) Not published as a crush question. The documented risk is chemical, not mechanical [3][4] Fat does not sublimate. Harvest Right names cheese, bacon, sausage, butter, peanut butter, salmon and avocados as items that "can still be freeze dried successfully, but they typically won't store as long" [3]. Sausages are separately "susceptible to case-hardening" [8] Not addressed for these items specifically. High-fat cheese is instead handled at prep: melt or blend and spread thinly before drying [8]

The fat problem

This is the part of a trail menu that is well sourced, and it has nothing to do with crushing. Freeze drying removes water; it does not remove fat. Utah State University Extension states the mechanism directly: "fat does not freeze like water. This slows the process and increases the risk of spoilage" [8]. Harvest Right's phrasing of the same point is that fat "does not freeze dry the same way moisture does" [3].

Four independent tiers agree on the consequence and none of them publishes a number:

  • Extension. High fat "increases the risk of rancidity during storage"; high-fat cheeses should be melted or blended and spread thinly before drying [8]. University of Minnesota: "foods that are high in fat or oil may not freeze-dry well" [9].
  • Freeze-dryer manufacturer. "Foods that contain higher amounts of fat generally have shorter storage lives because fats can oxidize over time" [4], with the named list above [3].
  • A commercial pouch brand's own catalog. Backpacker's Pantry explains its three-year SKUs against its ten-year ones in one sentence: "Products with a shelf life of three years typically have higher fat or dairy content" [12]. That is the clearest market-side confirmation of the direction available.
  • Dehydrated meat, for scale only. NCHFP instructs trimming and discarding all fat from meat "because it becomes rancid quickly," and states that properly dried jerky "will keep at room temperature two weeks in a sealed container" [11]. That is a jerky figure for a different process. It is the only concrete fat-driven room-temperature number found anywhere, and it does not transfer to a freeze-dried pouch.

The two techniques anyone publishes are both removal, not compensation. For ground beef: drain and thoroughly rinse with water "to remove as much grease as possible" before freeze-drying [9]. For meat generally: trim visible fat and bone before portioning [20]. Neither source quantifies what the rinse buys you.

One thing not to misread on the trail: visible oil is not a failure signal by itself. A commercial freeze-dried brand tells buyers that "product may appear wet due to the oil content. This is normal and the product is completely freeze dried and safe to consume" [22]. And fat inside a composite dish is treated differently from fat on its own — foods that are nearly pure fat "don't freeze dry well on their own" but work "when they're part of a larger dish like a cookie, sauce, or full meal" [2].

No source at any tier publishes a fat-percentage ceiling, or a quantified shelf-life reduction per unit of fat. Anyone giving you one is estimating.

What extension says not to dry

Extension exclusion lists are shorter and blunter than manufacturer lists, and they do not include the composite-dish exception. What they publish:

  • Oily foods. UC Cooperative Extension: generally avoid oily foods including butter, peanut butter and chocolate [10]. Compare Harvest Right, which permits the same items inside a larger dish [2]. Unreconciled.
  • Emulsions. Salad dressings, mayonnaise and oils — emulsions "do not freeze evenly, and this can ruin their texture" [8]. Utah State separately notes that high-fat foods such as mayonnaise "do not freeze-dry well and can become unsafe" [8].
  • High-sugar foods. Sugar "holds onto water and resists moisture loss, prolonging drying and requiring more energy" [8]; honey, syrups and jams "become a sticky, difficult-to-handle mess during the process and cannot be reconstituted properly" [2].
  • Baked goods. University of Minnesota states that the equipment works well for fruits, vegetables, dairy and proteins "but not for foods that are high in fat, high in sugar or for baked goods" [9]. Bread and cake are inside that class-level exclusion; neither source names a lean loaf separately.
  • Dense-cased items. Sausages are "susceptible to case-hardening" [8].
  • Raw flour and raw dough [8].
  • Raw eggs and unpasteurized dairy, as a safety matter rather than a quality one. "Raw eggs can contain Salmonella that survives freeze-drying" [8]; UC ANR adds that if eggs are freeze-dried raw they should be labeled "raw" and properly heated before consumption [10]. Freeze drying is not a kill step — foods rehydrated before eating need one, such as cooking [8].

Harvest Right's framing runs the other way: "very few foods are completely unsuitable for freeze drying" [3]. Both positions are published. The difference matters most for a backpacking menu, because the items extension excludes — fat and sugar — are exactly the items calorie density pushes you toward.

Packaging for crush and puncture

Here is the finding that shapes this whole section: no packaging manufacturer checked publishes a burst strength, puncture resistance, oxygen transmission rate or moisture vapor transmission rate for a consumer mylar food pouch. Four were checked directly [14][15][16][17][18]. Mil thickness, and in one case foil-layer thickness in inches, are the only quantitative durability figures the industry publishes at all.

The published figures, with their units:

  • 7.5 mil MRE-style mylar pouch, three layers including a foil laminate, 8" × 6" × 4.5" [14]. Retail 10-count with 100cc absorbers included: $14.99, or $1.50 per pouch [14]. The same pouch by the case of 500: $149.00, or $0.298 per pouch, falling to $134.00 per case at 6–10 cases [15]. That is a 5.0× per-pouch spread on an identical bag, same vendor, same day.
  • Mylar bag lines run 2.0 to 7.5 mil, with "Heavy Duty" grades starting at 7.0 mil; foil layer thickness is published as 0.00035" and 0.0005" against a stated competitor's 0.000285" [16]. The same seller claims "higher puncture resistance than any metalized polyester film" — a comparative claim with no force value behind it [16].
  • One seller publishes a floor rather than a spec: bags under 5 mil do not provide adequate protection from UV rays [17]. Its 0.01% figure is headspace oxygen after absorber use, not a transmission rate [17].
  • A packaging manufacturer selling into home freeze drying describes its pouch qualitatively as "strong, high barrier material" and directs enquirers to contact the company for datasheets [18].

Technique-level guidance is equally thin. The one published storage instruction that addresses puncture directly is to keep sealed mylar bags "in sturdy totes or storage bins" for protection from pests, accidental punctures and general wear [5] — which is a pantry instruction, not a pack instruction. Mountain House tells buyers to store its pouches away from any environment that could cause packaging damage "such as punctures or dents" [13]. No source, at any tier, addresses protecting a pouch inside a loaded backpack — not padding, not orientation, not where in the pack it should ride, not what compression does to a sealed bag. That absence is total.

It is subject to the same absence as everything else in this section — we can tell you the mil thickness the manufacturer publishes, and we cannot tell you a puncture rating for a bag in a loaded pack, because no manufacturer publishes one and we have not tested it.

What we could not source

  • A fragility ranking of freeze-dried foods. No source, primary or secondary, ranks food types by crush, shatter or compression risk. The leafy-greens line [1] is the sole primary statement, and one line is not an ordering.
  • Any numeric burst, puncture, OTR or MVTR value for a consumer mylar food pouch. Four packaging manufacturers checked directly [14][15][16][17][18]; zero numeric values found. No published ASTM F1140 or F1306 result for a consumer food pouch was located either.
  • Pack-carry technique. Padding, orientation, avoiding compression inside a loaded pack — nothing published by any brand, manufacturer or extension service.
  • A fat-percentage ceiling, or a shelf-life penalty per unit of fat. Every tier agrees on direction [3][4][8][9][12]; none publishes a number. The jerky two-week room-temperature figure [11] is a dehydrated-meat figure for a different process.
  • Whether crushed pieces rehydrate differently from intact ones. Nobody has tested it, and no source distinguishes the two.
  • Whether repackaging store-bought pouches into lighter bags changes durability. Unaddressed by every source checked.
  • Rehydration figures for beans and legumes, root vegetables specifically, or dairy and eggs. Harvest Right publishes general vegetable guidance [6] and no category breakdown.
  • Sublime Pantry has bench-tested none of this. Every figure above is somebody else's published claim, carrying its own units, conditions and publisher.
